description: Question: a river gage reads only the water level, yet USGS publishes the flow of the Missouri at Hermann every 15 minutes: where does the discharge come from, and how far can it be trusted? Idea: the stage-discharge rating curve. Hydrographers measure the discharge a few times a year (velocity across the section, by current meter or ADCP) and read the stage; a power law Q = C (h − e)^b through those measurements (e: the stage of zero flow, b: set by the hydraulic control, about 1.5–2.5 for a riffle or weir, 5/3 for a wide channel by Manning) turns every stage reading into a discharge. Here 4,117 field measurements since 1928 from the USGS Water Data API are fitted in Polars: for each e on a grid the fit is a straight line in log space, and the e with the least squared error wins (a profile likelihood gives its 95% interval, and with it how different the equally good curves are). Aha: the curve is a model with a shelf life. Fitted per decade, the stage that carries 40,000 ft³/s has fallen by more than 3 ft since the 1960s (bed degradation: sand dredging, and dams that trap sediment upstream), so one all-years curve under-reports today's low flows by over 40%, while floods barely move. And at the top, where the 100-year flood lives, the curve is weakest: 51% of the measurements are below 10 ft and only 65 at 30 ft or more; the one power law reads the 1993 record stage (36.97 ft) as about 564,000 ft³/s against the published 750,000, and the 10 measurements at 34.5 ft or more range from 418,000 to 750,000 ft³/s at nearly the same stage (rising against falling floods, backwater, levee breaks), while the curve's statistical interval there is only about 3%. Caveats: stage in ft above the gage datum (which may have changed), discharge in ft³/s; measurements are rated Excellent (2%) to Poor (>8%); hysteresis (rising floods carry more than falling ones at the same stage) and ice are not modelled; USGS's own rating uses segments and shifts, not one power law; peaks before 1928 are historic estimates. Next: other gages on the Missouri (Kansas City 06893000, St. Joseph 06818000) to see the degradation travel; the daily discharge (USGS daily collection) with the stage to see shifts applied; the flood frequency of the annual peaks.
name: River rating curve: the Missouri at Hermann
